s: PACCAR DEF 14A filed 2026-03-18, ownership table as of 2026-03-03; PCAR close 131.03 on 2026-08-21 (stockanalysis.com)
m: 3,490,462 PACCAR shares beneficially owned x $131.03 = $457M. Includes 75,567 deferred stock units in the director plan and shares held by spouse/children he disclaims.
did: Fourth-generation holder of the Pigott family block in PACCAR, the Bellevue maker of Kenworth, Peterbilt and DAF trucks. Spent 12 years inside the company, five running truck operations in the UK and US, then became a partner in Beta Capital Group in 2003 and now Beta Business Ventures in Seattle.
why: PACCAR sells premium trucks at premium prices and books the credit spread through PACCAR Financial, so it earns twice on the same unit. The family has never diluted, so a sub-2 percent block compounds against a $69B market cap. PACCAR was profitable every year from 1939 except 2009.
obst: Class 8 trucking is violently cyclical. North American orders fell about 45 percent in 2009 and PACCAR posted its first annual loss in seven decades; the family held the block rather than sell into the trough, and the shares have since risen roughly tenfold.
turn: 2003, when he left operating roles at PACCAR and formed Beta Capital Group, turning an inherited single-stock position into a managed family capital base.

s: Zulily SC 14D9 filed 2015-09-01, merger consideration table; Zulily DEF 14A 2015-04-02 (age 42 as of that date)
m: 21,015,781 Zulily shares taken out by QVC at $9.375 cash plus 0.3098 QVCA per share: $197.0M cash plus 6,510,688 QVCA shares, $394.0M total per the 14D9. Cut for tax and for the post-2015 collapse in Qurate stock.
did: Co-founded flash-sale retailer Zulily in Seattle in 2009 with Blue Nile's Mark Vadon, after a decade as Blue Nile's CTO. Ran it from zero to $1.2B of revenue, a November 2013 IPO at a $2.6B valuation, and QVC's October 2015 takeover at $18.75 a share, where his own stake fetched $394.0M in cash and Qurate stock.
why: Zulily inverted retail working capital. It ran a new flash event every morning, took the orders, and only then bought from the vendor, so it held almost no inventory and collected cash before it paid for goods. That let a startup reach $1.2B of revenue in five years on very little capital.
obst: The sell-then-buy model that made the balance sheet work also meant customers waited two to three weeks for orders. Churn rose after the IPO and the stock fell from about $73 to under $12 in 18 months, wiping out most of the public-market premium before QVC bid.
turn: August 2015, when Cavens accepted QVC's $18.75 a share rather than try to fix delivery times as a public company; the deal closed in October and locked in the value the stock had already given back.

s: Nordstrom PREM14A 2025, beneficial ownership as of 2025-01-31 and Annex D rollover schedule; take-private closed May 2025 at $24.25 per share
m: 12,068,673 shares beneficially owned x $24.25 merger price = $293M. Includes family trusts over which he shares voting power and which also appear in his brother Peter's count, so treat as an upper bound on his own economic interest.
did: Fourth-generation co-CEO of Nordstrom. Led the family buyout of the retailer his great-grandfather started as a Seattle shoe store in 1901: agreed December 2024, closed May 2025 at $24.25 a share and $6.25B, family 50.1 percent and Mexico's El Puerto de Liverpool 49.9. He rolled in 2,602,277 of his own shares.
why: Going private removed the quarterly comp-store scoreboard that forced Nordstrom to defend full-line stores it no longer needed. Liverpool supplied half the equity without demanding control, so the family kept the voting majority and the brand without the leverage a sponsor buyout would have loaded on.
obst: A first family bid in 2017-18 collapsed when the independent committee rejected $50 a share as too low; the pandemic then closed every store, the stock fell under $12, and the family had to come back seven years later and buy the same company at half its own rejected price.
turn: December 23, 2024, when the independent committee accepted $24.25 and the Liverpool partnership, ending 53 years of Nordstrom as a public company.

s: Apptio DEFM14A filed 2018-12-11, merger consideration table; Apptio DEF 14A 2018 (age 47)
m: $199,966,984 total merger consideration at $38.00 a share: 4,271,810 shares ($162.3M), 1,086,400 options ($31.6M), 127,000 RSUs and 31,000 PSUs. Net of tax, plus rollover equity realised when IBM bought Apptio from Vista for $4.6B in 2023.
did: Founded Apptio in Bellevue in 2007 to sell technology business management software that tells a CIO what each IT service actually costs. Took it public in 2016, sold it to Vista Equity in January 2019 at $38 a share where his stake cashed out at $200.0M, stayed on as CEO, and sold Apptio again to IBM for $4.6B in 2023.
why: Apptio reconciled general-ledger cost data to IT services, a mapping no ERP vendor maintained. Once three years of a company's cost history lived in that model, it became the CIO's budget system of record and switching meant rebuilding the history, so renewal rates ran above 100 percent of prior-year value.
obst: The category did not exist, so Apptio had to fund a TBM Council standards body to manufacture buyers. It then IPO'd in 2016 at $16 into a market punishing slow-growth SaaS and traded below the offer price for much of two years before Vista bid.
turn: November 2018, when Vista offered $38 a share, a 53 percent premium, ending the public discount and letting Gupta rebuild under private ownership for a second, larger exit to IBM.

s: Immunome DEF 14A filed 2026-04-24 (age 65; 3,707,559 shares, 3.19%); Pfizer-Seagen merger at $229 per share, 2023; IMNM close 28.52 on 2026-08-21
m: 565,526 Seagen shares x $229 Pfizer cash price = $129.5M, plus 3,707,559 Immunome shares and options (strikes $1.35 to $12.92) worth roughly $75M net of strike at IMNM $28.52. Excludes decades of prior Seagen sales.
did: Co-founded Seattle Genetics in Bothell in 1997 and ran it for 25 years, turning antibody-drug conjugates into Adcetris and Padcev and a company Pfizer bought for $43B at $229 a share in 2023. Since October 2023 he has been chairman and CEO of Immunome, a Bothell oncology company now worth about $3.2B.
why: ADCs had been written off after Mylotarg failed. Seagen spent a decade on linker chemistry so the cytotoxin stayed bolted to the antibody in blood and released only inside the tumour. That vc-MMAE linker became the industry standard and was licensed to Roche, Astellas and Genmab, funding 14 product-less years.
obst: Fourteen years from founding to first approval, through the 2001 biotech funding winter, financed on partner royalties rather than product revenue. Siegall was then forced out of the company he built in May 2022 after a domestic-violence arrest.
turn: August 2011, when the FDA approved Adcetris for Hodgkin lymphoma, validating the linker platform and repricing every licensing deal Seagen had signed.

s: Microsoft DEF 14A filed 2025-10-21, holdings as of 2025-09-30; MSFT close 483.24 on 2026-08-21 (stockanalysis.com)
m: 402,131 shares plus 26,151 unvested stock units = 428,282 x $483.24 = $207M. A floor: it excludes more than two decades of prior share sales, which are not netted out here.
did: Joined Microsoft in 1993 from Covington and Burling, became general counsel in 2002, president in 2015 and vice chair in 2021. Negotiated the settlements that ended the US state antitrust cases and the EU proceedings, and built the government-affairs and AI-policy machine Microsoft now runs.
why: Smith turned the legal department from a defence cost into a market-access function. Settling with Sun, Novell, RealNetworks, IBM, the US states and Brussels between 2002 and 2009 cleared the regulatory overhang on bundling, which is exactly the freedom Azure, Office 365 and Teams were later sold on.
obst: He inherited a company that had already lost. A federal court had ordered a breakup, the EU issued a $1.35B fine in 2008, and every rival was suing. Paying out and conceding rather than appealing was unpopular internally and cost Microsoft billions in cash settlements.
turn: 2002, when he took over as general counsel and reversed a decade of litigate-everything strategy, telling the board it was time to make peace.

s: Concur DEF 14A filed 2014-01-30 (age 52; 1,081,031 shares, 1.7%, 260,656 unvested RSUs); SAP acquisition at $129 per share, closed December 2014
m: 1,081,031 shares plus 260,656 unvested RSUs cashed at SAP's $129 offer = about $173M gross in December 2014, net of tax and before earlier open-market sales. Compounded modestly since.
did: Co-founded Concur as Portable Software in Bellevue in 1993 and was CEO from 1996. Rebuilt a boxed expense-report product into a hosted network and sold it to SAP for $8.3B at $129 a share in December 2014, where his own 1.08M shares and unvested units were worth about $173M.
why: The moat was the supplier network, not the software. Concur wired airlines, hotel chains and card issuers straight into the expense report, so itineraries and card charges arrived pre-filled. A rival had to rebuild hundreds of integrations, and the customer's travel policy was enforced inside Concur's workflow.
obst: The licensed business collapsed in the dot-com bust. Concur shares fell to roughly $0.31 in 2001, the company cut about a third of its staff, and Singh had to rewrite the entire product as a hosted service while revenue fell.
turn: 2001-2002, when Singh killed the shrink-wrap licence business outright and moved every customer to the hosted model, trading near-term revenue for recurring subscriptions.

s: Amazon DEF 14A filed 2026 (528,960 shares); Amazon 10-K for FY2025 executive officer table (age 59); AMZN close 258.63 on 2026-08-21
m: 528,960 shares per the proxy ownership table x $258.63 = $137M. Excludes unvested RSUs, which are the bulk of his annual pay, and excludes 20 years of prior sales.
did: CEO of Worldwide Amazon Stores since July 2022, running the whole retail business. Joined Amazon in May 2005 to start Consumables, built Subscribe and Save, ran North America Consumer from 2015, and after 2022 regionalised the US fulfilment network into eight self-sufficient zones to cut cost to serve.
why: Consumables is why Prime works. Cheap, heavy, high-frequency household goods gave customers a reason to order weekly rather than monthly, and that order density is what makes same-day delivery economics and the advertising business sitting on top of them possible at all.
obst: Consumables is the worst category in retail: low price, low margin, high shipping weight. He had to invent Subscribe and Save and the add-on item rule to make sub-$10 goods shippable at a profit, and Amazon's grocery push was shut down and restarted more than once.
turn: July 2022, when Jassy put all of worldwide stores under him and he broke the single national fulfilment network into eight regions, cutting the distance a typical package travels.

s: Smartsheet DEFM14A filed 2024-11-14, equity treatment and ownership tables; Smartsheet DEF 14A 2024-05-01 (age 53); merger closed 2025-01-22 at $56.50 per share
m: 675,012 shares at $56.50 ($38.1M) plus $84.0M of option, RSU and PSU consideration in the Blackstone-Vista buyout = about $122M gross. Net of tax, plus $9.7M realised on 2024 exercises and vestings.
did: CEO of Smartsheet from 2006, when it was a handful of people in Bellevue. Took the work-management company public in 2018 and sold it to Blackstone and Vista in January 2025 at $56.50 a share, an $8.4B deal in which his own shares and options were cashed out for about $122M.
why: Smartsheet won because it looked like a spreadsheet. Enterprises ran thousands of processes in Excel; Smartsheet kept the grid but added workflow, approvals and permissions, so an operations manager could adopt it on a credit card and it spread department by department without IT ever signing a purchase order.
obst: Smartsheet raised its first institutional round seven years after founding and had to convert a self-serve, credit-card product into an enterprise sales motion after the 2018 IPO. It burned cash on that conversion into fiscal 2024 and the stock spent 2022-2024 well below its 2021 high.
turn: 2012-2013, when Mader stopped selling to individuals and rebuilt around enterprise teams, raising average contract value roughly tenfold and making the later IPO possible.

s: Smartsheet DEF 14A filed 2024-05-01 (2,128,860 shares, 1.55%); Smartsheet DEF 14A 2021-05-05 (age 55); merger closed 2025-01-22 at $56.50 per share
m: 2,128,860 shares, of which 1,999,459 are outright Class A stock, x $56.50 cash merger price = $120.3M. Cash-settled, so no valuation modelling needed; small deduction for tax offsets prior sales.
did: Founded Smartsheet in 2005 and wrote its first version, after building Onyx Software into a CRM vendor that IPO'd in 1999. Was a Smartsheet employee to 2016 and a director to 2024, and held 2,128,860 shares taken out for $120.3M cash when Blackstone and Vista bought the company in January 2025.
why: Frei's bet was that business software fails when it asks people to abandon the grid. Smartsheet put a database and a workflow engine behind a spreadsheet UI, so it needed no training, spread horizontally inside companies, and did not compete for the IT budget that Microsoft Project already owned.
obst: His first company, Onyx Software, went public in 1999 near the top and then collapsed in the dot-com bust, eventually selling in 2006 for roughly $92M. Frei started Smartsheet in that wreckage and ran it on almost no outside money for its first seven years.
turn: 2006, when Frei recruited Mark Mader from Onvia to take the CEO seat while he stayed on product; the handoff is what let Smartsheet build an enterprise sales organisation he had no appetite to run.

s: Avalara DEFM14A filed 2022-09-06, ownership and equity treatment tables; Avalara DEF 14A 2022-04-21 (age 65); Vista deal closed 2022-10-19 at $93.50 per share
m: 1,045,851 shares and exercisable options (661k of which are options with strikes) x $93.50, plus $29.1M of unvested options, RSUs and PSUs cashed in the merger. About $105M gross after option strikes, before tax and prior sales.
did: Co-founded Avalara on Bainbridge Island in 2004 to automate US sales-tax calculation, returns and remittance across roughly 13,000 taxing jurisdictions. Took it public in June 2018 and sold it to Vista Equity in October 2022 at $93.50 a share, an $8.4B deal, having been chairman and CEO throughout.
why: The asset is content, not code: rate, boundary and taxability rules for every jurisdiction, maintained continuously, plus the filing itself. South Dakota v. Wayfair in June 2018 made economic nexus law in 45 states, converting a nice-to-have into a legal requirement for every online seller overnight.
obst: For 14 years Avalara sold something most merchants could legally ignore, because pre-Wayfair a seller owed tax only where it had physical presence. It raised round after round and stayed unprofitable while waiting for a law that might never change.
turn: June 21, 2018, when the Supreme Court decided Wayfair three days after Avalara's IPO; the addressable market went from thousands of sellers to millions and the stock roughly tripled inside a year.
